title: I Let the Community Cider-Press Booking Hit the Chair Who Left Our Apples in the Hopper

parts.text: I arrived at the community press at 9:03 a.m. and chair Nolan had our numbered crates already in the hopper. The sheet said: TWO HOURS. HOPPER CLEARS WITH THE BOOKING. I was forty-one, orchard volunteer, holding a wash ticket that listed our lot. Nolan shrugged. "Chairs are the mill." I photographed the sheet, the crates, and his pomace on our cloth. Then I asked for the press log. At 9:11 facilities pinged why Nolan's name was on our mash. I kept my voice barn-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A cloth is only a cloth until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: Facilities can see Nolan's mash in the hopper during our booking.

social.video_title: He left our apples in the hopper on our slot — Part 1/2
social.description: Cider press, a chair on our cloth, a two-hour clock he posted. I logged the mash. Would you have asked for the press log?

parts.text: Nolan called it a rinse until facilities asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the sheet, and the cloth still. The hopper went back to our lot. Nolan ran his own two hours and told the next chair atmosphere was always about yield. Yield is a word chairs use when a booking exists. Press policy now has a second line: CHAIRS ARE NOT THE MILL. I keep our cloth on a labeled peg. Nolan brown-bags his jokes. The mill finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Chairs are not the mill — Part 2/2
social.description: Press log, numbered crates, and a second line on the sheet. Was a rinse ever our cloth?
